heading: Abstract
text:
\nThis paper develops the angular and static-channel component of Geometric and Spectral Alignment for residual Jacobian chains. Starting from Cartan-coordinate rigidity and fitted effective-rank windows, we study how dominant singular subspaces are transported across adjacent layers and how the resulting finite matrices can be displayed in physical channel coordinates.
    
\nThe main results are deterministic, margin-verified results. We bound the error between full interface transport and its dominant-window truncation, add fitted-tail errors so that empirical spectra can be certified against the Gibbs–Cartan tail model, and distinguish source-mode incidence from fully physical input-output channel incidence. Given row groups and active supports, the Physical Alignment Matrix decomposes orthogonally as core plus overlap plus noise. Active-column gaps, pairwise overlap margins, and noise bounds combine into a static certificate radius under which the full transport and the truncated transport induce the same active supports, pairwise incidence graph, SRS sets, hub columns, and core/overlap/noise masks. The finer SC/SA/ST labels of the Invariant Channel Mapping require additional row-energy and profile-correlation margins, stated as explicit perturbation tests.
    
\nThe empirical section reports the matrices and block-energy heatmaps that measure these certificate quantities across CNNs, language models, and vision/diffusion backbones. The figures are interpreted as finite-dimensional measurements; complete membership in the Physical GSA certificate domain requires checking the numerical margin protocol stated in Section 10.

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
\n
\nThe spectral article proves that a budgeted residual Jacobian cocycle has a short Cartan-coordinate path and, under a positive rank-separation margin, a stable dominant energy window. This paper studies the angular geometry inside that window. The singular values of a layer specify how much energy is carried by each mode; the singular vectors specify how those modes are routed through the next layer. The resulting angular transport is the finite-dimensional object seen in physical channel coordinates, and it is closely related to residual-Jacobian alignment phenomena observed in residual networks [7] and to classical subspace-angle geometry [1].

\n
\nThe basic matrix data are as follows. For a layer matrix W=U​Σ​V⊤W=U\Sigma V^{\top}, the columns of UU are output singular directions, the columns of VV are input singular directions, and the diagonal entries of Σ\Sigma are singular amplitudes. After selecting an effective-rank window, adjacent layers provide two frames: the left singular frame of the current layer and the right singular frame of the next layer. Their overlap matrix, together with singular-value weights and physical output realization, produces the transport matrices used in the paper. A row/column permutation then displays the same transport in channel coordinates.

\n
\nThe objects developed here are finite-dimensional and directly computable from static matrices. Given two adjacent layer maps with singular-vector frames, we form angular transport matrices and energy-weighted variants. Mode-profile row groups and active support margins then determine a Physical Alignment Matrix, pairwise relational triples, and a global decomposition


\n

M^phy=Mcore+Moverlap+Mnoise.\widehat{M}_{\mathrm{phy}}=M_{\mathrm{core}}+M_{\mathrm{overlap}}+M_{\mathrm{noise}}.


\nThis decomposition records which output channel groups connect to which declared column supports, which supports are shared, and which residual mass is not structured by the selected dominant window. When the selected transport has source-mode columns these are mode supports; when it has physical-input columns they are physical channel supports.

\n
\nThe main certificate implication proved in this paper is


\n

stable spectral window\displaystyle\text{stable spectral window}
⟹controlled truncated physical transport\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\text{controlled truncated physical transport}

\n


⟹margin-stable static incidence and support-level ICM.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\text{margin-stable static incidence and support-level ICM}.


\nThe same finite-dimensional coordinates also give a mathematical form of low-disruption fine-tuning: scale perturbations with small relative-ratio cost are close to uniform layerwise scaling, and small SVD-frame perturbations require the left and right singular-vector rotations to remain coherent up to explicitly controlled relative-rotation error. This provides a coordinate system in which one can test whether a particular adapter or low-rank adaptation update is low-disruption; no claim is made that those methods automatically satisfy the stated margins.

\n
\nThe experiments are organized by the quantities in the theorems; visual block structure is treated as a measurement of certificate variables rather than as proof of domain membership by itself. Physical alignment matrices and block-energy heatmaps measure the finite matrices, row/column partitions, noise residuals, and pairwise margins that appear in the statements. The displayed block-dominant patterns are consistent with the structural behavior predicted by the theory; a stronger finite-dimensional margin check additionally reports the active gaps, noise bounds, and pairwise margin values stated in the hypotheses.

heading: 2 Spectral input and finite-dimensional notation
text:
\n
\nThis section records the spectral notation used by the angular theory and proves the finite-dimensional estimates used later in the paper. The arguments are included here so that the angular and static-channel theory can be read independently of the companion spectral article.

heading: 2.1 Minimal matrix-geometric notation for angular transport
text:
\n
\nAll objects in this article are finite-dimensional. The real general linear group is


\n

GL⁡(d):={A∈ℝd×d:detA≠0},\mathrm{GL}(d):=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:\det A\neq 0\},


\nand the orthogonal group is


\n

O⁡(d):={Q∈ℝd×d:Q⊤​Q=I}.\mathrm{O}(d):=\{Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:Q^{\top}Q=\mathrm{I}\}.


\nFor a full-rank layer matrix A∈GL⁡(d)A\in\mathrm{GL}(d), the positive form A⊤​AA^{\top}A belongs to


\n

SPD⁡(d):={P=P⊤:x⊤​P​x>0​ for every ​x≠0}.\mathrm{SPD}(d):=\{P=P^{\top}:x^{\top}Px>0\text{ for every }x\neq 0\}.


\nThe map A↦A⊤​AA\mapsto A^{\top}A removes the left orthogonal gauge, since (Q​A)⊤​(Q​A)=A⊤​A(QA)^{\top}(QA)=A^{\top}A for every Q∈O⁡(d)Q\in\mathrm{O}(d). Thus singular values are quotient-radial data, while singular vectors are angular data depending on the chosen input and output frames.

\n
\nFor an SVD W=U​Σ​V⊤W=U\Sigma V^{\top}, the output frame UU and input frame VV determine subspaces in the physical channel coordinates. The overlap between two RR-dimensional orthonormal frames X,Y∈ℝd×RX,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times R} is measured by X⊤​YX^{\top}Y; the singular values of this matrix are the cosines of the principal angles between the two subspaces [1]. The angular transport matrices below are weighted and physically realized versions of such subspace-overlap matrices. In a neural layer, this means that they record how dominant output modes of one transformation are received by the input modes or physical output channels of the next transformation.

\n

\nLet W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and set d=max⁡{m,n}d=\max\{m,n\}. Define W~∈ℝd×d\widetilde{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} by

(1)

\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nIf m≤nm\leq n, then d=nd=n and W~\widetilde{W} is obtained by adding n−mn-m zero rows below WW. Therefore


\n

W~⊤​W~=W⊤​W.\widetilde{W}^{\top}\widetilde{W}=W^{\top}W.


\nThe matrix W⊤​WW^{\top}W has dimension n×nn\times n; its eigenvalues are the mm squared singular values of WW together with n−mn-m zeros. Hence the nn singular values of the square matrix W~\widetilde{W} are the singular values of WW together with n−m=|m−n|n-m=|m-n| additional zeros.

\n
\nIf m>nm>n, then d=md=m and W~\widetilde{W} is obtained by adding m−nm-n zero columns to WW. Then


\n

W~⊤​W~=[W⊤​W000],\widetilde{W}^{\top}\widetilde{W}=\begin{bmatrix}W^{\top}W&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix},


\nwhere the lower-right zero block has size (m−n)×(m−n)(m-n)\times(m-n). Thus the eigenvalues of W~⊤​W~\widetilde{W}^{\top}\widetilde{W} are those of W⊤​WW^{\top}W together with m−nm-n additional zeros, and taking nonnegative square roots proves the singular-value statement.

\n
\nThe operator norm is the largest singular value and the Frobenius norm is the square root of the sum of squared singular values. Since the only added singular values are zero, both norms are unchanged.
∎

heading: 2.2 Spectral tail geometry and compressibility
text:
\n
\nThe compressibility part of the theory is best formulated as a spectral-tail quantity rather than only as a rank statistic but as a tail problem for a probability measure on the rank set.
Along the Cartan power-law orbit, this measure is exactly the Gibbs family already introduced above.
The effective rank is therefore an energy-truncation quantile of a spectral tail measure.

\n

heading: Definition 2.14 (Spectral energy measure and truncation rank).
text:
\n
\nLet WW have a declared spectral fitting list of length d=dsp​(W)d=d_{\mathrm{sp}}(W) with singular values σ1​(W)≥⋯≥σd​(W)≥0 igma_{1}(W)\geq\cdots\geq igma_{d}(W)\geq 0, excluding any square-embedding padding zeros unless they are part of the declared numerical spectrum.
Define the spectral energy measure


\n

μW:=∑i=1dσi​(W)2‖W‖F2​δi,\mu_{W}:= um_{i=1}^{d}\frac{ igma_{i}(W)^{2}}{\|W\|_{F}^{2}}\,\delta_{i},


\na probability measure on {1,…,d}\{1,\dots,d\}.
For 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, define the truncation rank


\n

Rε​(W):=min⁡{r∈{1,…,d}:μW​({1,…,r})≥1−ε}.R_{\varepsilon}(W):=\min\Bigl\{r\in\{1,\dots,d\}:\mu_{W}(\{1,\dots,r\})\geq 1-\varepsilon\Bigr\}.


\nEquivalently,


\n

Rε​(W)=min⁡{r:∑i=1rσi​(W)2≥(1−ε)​∑i=1dσi​(W)2}.R_{\varepsilon}(W)=\min\left\{r: um_{i=1}^{r} igma_{i}(W)^{2}\geq(1-\varepsilon) um_{i=1}^{d} igma_{i}(W)^{2}\right\}.




\n

heading: Remark 2.15 (Geometric interpretation).
text:
\n
\nThe quantity Rε​(W)R_{\varepsilon}(W) is the smallest spectral truncation at which the projected Gram point W⊤​WW^{\top}W retains at least (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon) of its total energy.
It is therefore a quantile of a spectral measure rather than a combinatorial surrogate for rank.
For rectangular layers, this rank refers to the spectral fitting list in Definition 2.2, while the resulting singular vectors may still be embedded into physical display coordinates when transport matrices are formed.


\n

heading: Definition 2.16 (Power-law tail measure on the Gibbs–Cartan orbit).
text:
\n
\nUnder the exact power-law model σi​(W)=C​i−α igma_{i}(W)=Ci^{-\alpha}, define


\n

να:=∑i=1di−2​αHd,2​α​δi.\nu_{\alpha}:= um_{i=1}^{d}\frac{i^{-2\alpha}}{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}}\,\delta_{i}.


\nThen μW=να\mu_{W}=\nu_{\alpha}.
For r∈{0,1,…,d}r\in\{0,1,\dots,d\}, define the tail function


\n

τα​(r):=να​({r+1,…,d})=Hd,2​α−Hr,2​αHd,2​α,\tau_{\alpha}(r):=\nu_{\alpha}(\{r+1,\dots,d\})=\frac{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}-\mathrm{H}_{r,2\alpha}}{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}},


\nwith the convention H0,s:=0\mathrm{H}_{0,s}:=0; thus τα​(0)=1\tau_{\alpha}(0)=1 and τα​(d)=0\tau_{\alpha}(d)=0.


\n

heading: Lemma 2.17 (Integral bounds for power-law tails).
text:
\n
\nLet s>0s>0 and 1≤r<d1\leq r<d. Then


\n

∫r+1d+1x−s​𝑑x≤∑i=r+1di−s≤∫rdx−s​𝑑x.\int_{r+1}^{d+1}x^{-s}\,dx\leq um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-s}\leq\int_{r}^{d}x^{-s}\,dx.

(7)

\nIf s>1s>1, then


\n

∑i=r+1di−s≤∫r∞x−s​𝑑x=r1−ss−1. um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-s}\leq\int_{r}^{\infty}x^{-s}\,dx=\frac{r^{1-s}}{s-1}.

(8)



\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nLet f⁡(x):=x−sf(x):=x^{-s}. For s>0s>0, ff is positive and decreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty). For every integer i≥1i\geq 1, monotonicity gives


\n

∫ii+1f⁡(x)​𝑑x≤f⁡(i)≤∫i−1if⁡(x)​𝑑x.\int_{i}^{i+1}f(x)\,dx\leq f(i)\leq\int_{i-1}^{i}f(x)\,dx.


\nApply the left inequality with i=r+1,…,di=r+1,\ldots,d and sum to obtain


\n

∫r+1d+1x−s​𝑑x=∑i=r+1d∫ii+1x−s​𝑑x≤∑i=r+1di−s.\int_{r+1}^{d+1}x^{-s}\,dx= um_{i=r+1}^{d}\int_{i}^{i+1}x^{-s}\,dx\leq um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-s}.


\nApply the right inequality with the same indices and sum to obtain


\n

∑i=r+1di−s≤∑i=r+1d∫i−1ix−s​𝑑x=∫rdx−s​𝑑x. um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-s}\leq um_{i=r+1}^{d}\int_{i-1}^{i}x^{-s}\,dx=\int_{r}^{d}x^{-s}\,dx.


\nThis proves (7). If s>1s>1, the improper integral converges, and the already established upper bound gives


\n

∑i=r+1di−s≤∫rdx−s​𝑑x≤∫r∞x−s​𝑑x=[x1−s1−s]x=r∞=r1−ss−1. um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-s}\leq\int_{r}^{d}x^{-s}\,dx\leq\int_{r}^{\infty}x^{-s}\,dx=\left[\frac{x^{1-s}}{1-s}\right]_{x=r}^{\infty}=\frac{r^{1-s}}{s-1}.


\nThis is (8).
∎


\n

heading: Theorem 2.18 (Energy truncation on the Gibbs–Cartan tail).
text:
\n
\nLet W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} satisfy the exact power-law model


\n

σi​(W)=C​i−α,α>12. igma_{i}(W)=C\,i^{-\alpha},\qquad\alpha>\frac{1}{2}.


\nThen μW=να\mu_{W}=\nu_{\alpha}, and the truncation rank from Definition 2.14 is


\n

Rε​(W)=min⁡{r:τα​(r)≤ε}.R_{\varepsilon}(W)=\min\{r:\tau_{\alpha}(r)\leq\varepsilon\}.


\nMoreover, for every r∈{1,…,d−1}r\in\{1,\dots,d-1\},


\n

Hd,2​α−Hr,2​α≤r1−2​α2​α−1,\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}-\mathrm{H}_{r,2\alpha}\leq\frac{r^{1-2\alpha}}{2\alpha-1},

(9)

\nhence


\n

Rε​(W)≤min⁡{d,⌈(1(2​α−1)​ε​Hd,2​α)12​α−1⌉}.R_{\varepsilon}(W)\leq\min\left\{d,\;\left\lceil\left(\frac{1}{(2\alpha-1)\,\varepsilon\,\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\alpha-1}}\right\rceil\right\}.

(10)

\nConversely, if r∈{1,…,d−1}r\in\{1,\dots,d-1\} satisfies


\n

(r+1)1−2​α−(d+1)1−2​α2​α−1≥ε​Hd,2​α,\frac{(r+1)^{1-2\alpha}-(d+1)^{1-2\alpha}}{2\alpha-1}\geq\varepsilon\,\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha},

(11)

\nthen


\n

Rε​(W)>r.R_{\varepsilon}(W)>r.




\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nSince μW=να\mu_{W}=\nu_{\alpha}, one has


\n

τα​(r)=∑i=r+1dC2​i−2​α∑i=1dC2​i−2​α=Hd,2​α−Hr,2​αHd,2​α.\tau_{\alpha}(r)=\frac{ um_{i=r+1}^{d}C^{2}i^{-2\alpha}}{ um_{i=1}^{d}C^{2}i^{-2\alpha}}=\frac{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}-\mathrm{H}_{r,2\alpha}}{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}}.


\nThus Rε​(W)R_{\varepsilon}(W) is exactly the smallest rr with τα​(r)≤ε\tau_{\alpha}(r)\leq\varepsilon.
Applying Lemma 2.17 with s=2​α>1s=2\alpha>1 gives


\n

Hd,2​α−Hr,2​α=∑i=r+1di−2​α≤∫r∞x−2​α​𝑑x=r1−2​α2​α−1,\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}-\mathrm{H}_{r,2\alpha}= um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-2\alpha}\leq\int_{r}^{\infty}x^{-2\alpha}\,dx=\frac{r^{1-2\alpha}}{2\alpha-1},


\nwhich proves (9).
If the right-hand side is at most ε​Hd,2​α\varepsilon\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}, then τα​(r)≤ε\tau_{\alpha}(r)\leq\varepsilon, hence Rε​(W)≤rR_{\varepsilon}(W)\leq r, giving (10).
The lower bound follows from the lower integral estimate


\n

∑i=r+1di−2​α≥∫r+1d+1x−2​α​𝑑x=(r+1)1−2​α−(d+1)1−2​α2​α−1, um_{i=r+1}^{d}i^{-2\alpha}\geq\int_{r+1}^{d+1}x^{-2\alpha}\,dx=\frac{(r+1)^{1-2\alpha}-(d+1)^{1-2\alpha}}{2\alpha-1},


\nwhich implies τα​(r)≥ε\tau_{\alpha}(r)\geq\varepsilon under (11).
∎


\n

heading: Remark 2.19 (Large-width scaling).
text:
\n
\nFor fixed α>12\alpha>\frac{1}{2} and large dd, Hd,2​α→ζ⁡(2​α)\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}\to\zeta(2\alpha).
The upper bound in Theorem 2.18 therefore gives the explicit leading scale


\n

Rε​(W)≤⌈(1+o⁡(1)(2​α−1)​ε​ζ​(2​α))12​α−1⌉(d→∞).R_{\varepsilon}(W)\leq\left\lceil\left(\frac{1+o(1)}{(2\alpha-1)\varepsilon\,\zeta(2\alpha)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\alpha-1}}\right\rceil\qquad(d\to\infty).


\nThe theorem above is its exact finite-width form on the Gibbs–Cartan orbit.


\n

heading: Proposition 2.20 (Monotonicity of truncation rank along the Cartan orbit).
text:
\n
\nFix 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 and finite width dd.
For the power-law tail measures να\nu_{\alpha} from Definition 2.16, the cumulative mass


\n

Fr​(α):=να​({1,…,r})=∑i=1ri−2​αHd,2​αF_{r}(\alpha):=\nu_{\alpha}(\{1,\dots,r\})= um_{i=1}^{r}\frac{i^{-2\alpha}}{\mathrm{H}_{d,2\alpha}}


\nis nondecreasing in α\alpha for every r=1,…,dr=1,\dots,d.
Equivalently, the tail mass τα​(r)=1−Fr​(α)\tau_{\alpha}(r)=1-F_{r}(\alpha) is nonincreasing in α\alpha.
Consequently, the truncation rank Rε​(α):=min⁡{r:τα​(r)≤ε}R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha):=\min\{r:\tau_{\alpha}(r)\leq\varepsilon\} is nonincreasing as a function of α\alpha.


\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nFix rr and write A={1,…,r}A=\{1,\dots,r\}.
Using the Gibbs form pi(α)∝e−2​α​log⁡ip_{i}^{(\alpha)}\propto e^{-2\alpha\log i},


\n

dd​α​pi(α)=−2​(log⁡i−Ud​(α))​pi(α).\frac{d}{d\alpha}p_{i}^{(\alpha)}=-2\bigl(\log i-U_{d}(\alpha)\bigr)p_{i}^{(\alpha)}.


\nTherefore


\n

Fr′(α)=−2∑i∈A(logi−Ud(α))pi(α)=2Fr(α)(Ud(α)−𝔼p(α)[logi∣i∈A]),F_{r}^{\prime}(\alpha)=-2 um_{i\in A}(\log i-U_{d}(\alpha))p_{i}^{(\alpha)}=2F_{r}(\alpha)\left(U_{d}(\alpha)-\mathbb{E}_{p^{(\alpha)}}[\log i\mid i\in A]\right),


\nwith the convention that the derivative is zero when Fr​(α)=0F_{r}(\alpha)=0, which never occurs here.
The conditional mean over AA is at most the unconditional mean Ud​(α)U_{d}(\alpha), because every value of log⁡i\log i on AcA^{c} is at least every value on AA.
Hence Fr′​(α)≥0F_{r}^{\prime}(\alpha)\geq 0.
Thus τα​(r)=1−Fr​(α)\tau_{\alpha}(r)=1-F_{r}(\alpha) is nonincreasing in α\alpha.
If α2≥α1\alpha_{2}\geq\alpha_{1} and r=Rε​(α1)r=R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}), then τα2​(r)≤τα1​(r)≤ε\tau_{\alpha_{2}}(r)\leq\tau_{\alpha_{1}}(r)\leq\varepsilon, so Rε​(α2)≤r=Rε​(α1)R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{2})\leq r=R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}).
∎


\n

heading: Lemma 2.21 (Uniform Lipschitz bound for spectral tail masses).
text:
\n
\nFor every r∈{0,1,…,d}r\in\{0,1,\dots,d\} and every α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0,


\n

|τα​(r)−τβ​(r)|≤2​(log⁡d)​|α−β|.|\tau_{\alpha}(r)-\tau_{\beta}(r)|\leq 2(\log d)|\alpha-\beta|.

(12)



\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nThe endpoints require no estimate: if r=0r=0, then τα​(0)=1\tau_{\alpha}(0)=1 for all α\alpha, and if r=dr=d, then τα​(d)=0\tau_{\alpha}(d)=0 for all α\alpha. In both cases the left-hand side of (12) is zero.

\n
\nAssume now 1≤r≤d−11\leq r\leq d-1 and set


\n

Fr​(α):=1−τα​(r)=∑i=1rpi(α).F_{r}(\alpha):=1-\tau_{\alpha}(r)= um_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}^{(\alpha)}.


\nThe derivative calculation in Proposition 2.20 gives


\n

Fr′​(α)=2​Fr​(α)​(Ud​(α)−𝔼p(α)​[log⁡i∣i≤r]).F_{r}^{\prime}(\alpha)=2F_{r}(\alpha)\left(U_{d}(\alpha)-\mathbb{E}_{p^{(\alpha)}}[\log i\mid i\leq r]\right).


\nThe factor Fr​(α)F_{r}(\alpha) lies in [0,1][0,1]. The random variable log⁡i\log i always lies in [0,log⁡d][0,\log d], so both the unconditional mean Ud​(α)U_{d}(\alpha) and the conditional mean 𝔼p(α)​[log⁡i∣i≤r]\mathbb{E}_{p^{(\alpha)}}[\log i\mid i\leq r] lie in that same interval. Therefore


\n

|Ud​(α)−𝔼p(α)​[log⁡i∣i≤r]|≤log⁡d.\left|U_{d}(\alpha)-\mathbb{E}_{p^{(\alpha)}}[\log i\mid i\leq r]\right|\leq\log d.


\nCombining the two bounds gives


\n

|Fr′​(α)|≤2​log⁡d.|F_{r}^{\prime}(\alpha)|\leq 2\log d.


\nSince τα​(r)=1−Fr​(α)\tau_{\alpha}(r)=1-F_{r}(\alpha), we also have


\n

|dd​α​τα​(r)|=|Fr′​(α)|≤2​log⁡d.\left|\frac{d}{d\alpha}\tau_{\alpha}(r)\right|=|F_{r}^{\prime}(\alpha)|\leq 2\log d.


\nFor arbitrary α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, the mean value theorem applied to the continuously differentiable function γ↦τγ​(r)\gamma\mapsto\tau_{\gamma}(r) gives


\n

|τα​(r)−τβ​(r)|≤supγ​ between ​α​ and ​β|dd​γ​τγ​(r)|​|α−β|≤2​(log⁡d)​|α−β|,|\tau_{\alpha}(r)-\tau_{\beta}(r)|\leq up_{\gamma\text{ between }\alpha\text{ and }\beta}\left|\frac{d}{d\gamma}\tau_{\gamma}(r)\right|\,|\alpha-\beta|\leq 2(\log d)|\alpha-\beta|,


\nwhich proves (12).
∎


\n

heading: Definition 2.22 (Rank-separation margin).
text:
\n
\nFix 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 and α>0\alpha>0.
Let rε​(α):=Rε​(α)r_{\varepsilon}(\alpha):=R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha) denote the truncation rank of the power-law energy measure να\nu_{\alpha}.
Define the rank-separation margin


\n

𝔪ε​(α):=min⁡{ε−τα​(rε​(α)),τα​(rε​(α)−1)−ε}.\mathfrak{m}_{\varepsilon}(\alpha):=\min\bigl\{\varepsilon-\tau_{\alpha}(r_{\varepsilon}(\alpha)),\ \tau_{\alpha}(r_{\varepsilon}(\alpha)-1)-\varepsilon\bigr\}.

(13)

\nThe margin is positive precisely when the threshold ε\varepsilon does not coincide with the tail mass at either side of the selected rank.


\n

heading: Definition 2.23 (Fitted-tail error).
text:
\n
\nLet W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} have spectral energy measure μW\mu_{W} and let α>0\alpha>0 be a fitted Cartan-tail parameter. Define the fitted-tail discrepancy


\n

Δtail​(W,α):=sup0≤r≤d|μW​({r+1,…,d})−τα​(r)|.\Delta_{\mathrm{tail}}(W,\alpha):= up_{0\leq r\leq d}\left|\mu_{W}(\{r+1,\ldots,d\})-\tau_{\alpha}(r)\right|.

(14)

\nThis quantity compares the actual empirical spectral tail of WW with the Gibbs–Cartan tail at parameter α\alpha. It is stronger than the chart error echarte^{\mathrm{chart}}, which only controls the top radial coordinate.


\n

heading: Proposition 2.24 (Robust empirical effective-rank window under fitted tails).
text:
\n
\nFix 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 and let r=Rε​(α)r=R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha) for the Gibbs–Cartan tail at parameter α\alpha. If


\n

Δtail​(W,α)<𝔪ε​(α),\Delta_{\mathrm{tail}}(W,\alpha)<\mathfrak{m}_{\varepsilon}(\alpha),

(15)

\nthen the empirical truncation rank of WW equals the fitted-tail rank:


\n

Rε​(W)=Rε​(α)=r.R_{\varepsilon}(W)=R_{\varepsilon}(\alpha)=r.

heading: 3 Activation permeability and conditional residual capacity
text:
\n
\nThis section is an optional capacity-accounting layer rather than a hypothesis needed for the static channel-incidence certificates below. The constants κϕ\kappa_{\phi} and χϕ\chi_{\phi} give activation-dependent sufficient conditions for residual-scale control. The main physical-alignment theory in Sections 4–8 is finite-dimensional and matrix-theoretic: its conclusions require the explicit spectral, truncation, active-support, pairwise-overlap, and noise margins stated there.

\n
\nThe spectral and angular geometry above describes static weight geometry.
To connect it to nonlinear residual networks, we introduce two activation-dependent constants.
They enter through explicit assumptions, and the resulting bounds are mathematically conditional and checkable. The definitions are compatible with the variance-propagation role of activation derivatives in Xavier/Glorot and He initialization, and with the smooth activations used in modern networks [2, 4, 5, 8].

\n

\n

\nThe scalar κϕ\kappa_{\phi} is the gradient permeability and χϕ\chi_{\phi} is the criticality capacity of the activation under the standard Gaussian input model.


\n

text:

The symbol κϕ\kappa_{\phi} is reserved exclusively for activation permeability.

heading: 3.1 Activation-capacity width bounds

heading: Proposition 3.5 (Activation-capacity width bounds as a capacity-accounting consequence).
text:
\n
\nFix a spectral block with effective output rank rout>0r_{\mathrm{out}}>0.
Let WW denote the number of physical input channels assigned to feed this block.
Assume that χϕ>0\chi_{\phi}>0 for the critical coherent regime and κϕ2>0\kappa_{\phi}^{2}>0 for the typical robust regime.
Assume the following capacity-accounting model.

\n(B1) 
\n
\nA stable realization of the block must supply at least routr_{\mathrm{out}} units of effective variance to its output subspace.

\n(B2) 
\n
\nIn the critical coherent regime, the total stable effective variance supplied by WW assigned input channels is at most W​χϕW\chi_{\phi}.

\n(B3) 
\n
\nIn the typical robust regime, the total stable effective variance supplied by WW assigned input channels is at most W​κϕ2W\kappa_{\phi}^{2}.


\nThen any critical coherent realization satisfies


\n

W≥routχϕ,W\geq\frac{r_{\mathrm{out}}}{\chi_{\phi}},

(25)

\nand any typical robust realization satisfies


\n

W≥routκϕ2.W\geq\frac{r_{\mathrm{out}}}{\kappa_{\phi}^{2}}.

\nEquivalently, the integer channel counts must obey

W≥⌈routχϕ⌉orW≥⌈routκϕ2⌉W\geq\left\lceil\frac{r_{\mathrm{out}}}{\chi_{\phi}}\right\rceil\quad\text{or}\quad W\geq\left\lceil\frac{r_{\mathrm{out}}}{\kappa_{\phi}^{2}}\right\rceil


\nin the two respective regimes.

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nThe proof is a deterministic capacity-counting argument. We keep the two regimes separate because they use different per-channel supply constants.

\n(W1) 
\n
\nCritical coherent regime.
By assumption (B2), the total critical coherent supply of the WW assigned channels satisfies


\n

total critical supply≤W​χϕ.\text{total critical supply}\leq W\chi_{\phi}.


\nBy assumption (B1), any stable realization of the block must supply at least routr_{\mathrm{out}} units to its effective output subspace. Therefore the necessary inequality is


\n

W​χϕ≥rout.W\chi_{\phi}\geq r_{\mathrm{out}}.


\nBy the positive-capacity assumption χϕ>0\chi_{\phi}>0, dividing by χϕ\chi_{\phi} gives


\n

W≥routχϕ,W\geq\frac{r_{\mathrm{out}}}{\chi_{\phi}},


\nwhich is (25).

\n(W2) 
\n
\nTypical robust regime.
Assumption (B3) gives the corresponding typical robust supply bound


\n

total typical supply≤W​κϕ2.\text{total typical supply}\leq W\kappa_{\phi}^{2}.


\nThe demand is still routr_{\mathrm{out}} by (B1). Hence


\n

\n

\nwhich is (26).

\n(W3) 
\n
\nInteger channel counts.
The variable WW counts physical input channels and is therefore an integer. If an integer WW satisfies W≥aW\geq a for a real number aa, then it also satisfies W≥⌈a⌉W\geq\lceil a\rceil. Applying this to a=rout/χϕa=r_{\mathrm{out}}/\chi_{\phi} and a=rout/κϕ2a=r_{\mathrm{out}}/\kappa_{\phi}^{2} gives the two ceiling forms.


\n∎

heading: Remark 3.6 (Conditional scope of the width bounds).
text:
\n
\nThe bounds are conditional on the capacity-accounting assumptions (B1)–(B3). Under those assumptions, no additional probabilistic independence or architectural heuristic is used in the proof; the inequalities are exact consequences of demand-versus-supply accounting. The constants κϕ\kappa_{\phi} and χϕ\chi_{\phi} are activation-dependent moments under the chosen input law and can be estimated numerically or analytically when the activation permits.

heading: 4 Angular transport and physical alignment
text:
\n
\nThe Cartan theory controls singular values after the orthogonal gauge has been removed.
The Physical GSA also requires a static description of how dominant singular directions are routed across an interface.
The description is formulated as a finite-dimensional static-structure theory: all objects are defined directly from SVD data and permutations, and every theorem below is a deterministic consequence of explicit margin inequalities.
Whether a trained network satisfies these margin inequalities is an empirical question measured in Section 10; the consequences of the inequalities are mathematical.

\n
\nThere are two logically distinct levels. First, the given-structure statements assume row groups, support sizes, and active column sets and then prove projection, pairwise-margin, and block-energy consequences. Second, the extraction statements use deterministic rules, such as mode-profile row assignment and top-energy active columns, and require row-profile gaps or active-column gaps to ensure that the extracted structure is stable under perturbation. Whenever a theorem claims preservation of an incidence structure, the relevant extraction gaps are stated explicitly; otherwise the statement is to be read with the row groups and active sets fixed.

heading: 4.1 Dominant angular transport matrices
text: \n

heading: Definition 4.1 (SVD gauge convention for angular transport).
text:
\n
\nFor every matrix whose singular vectors are used in the angular theory, fix once and for all a deterministic SVD selection rule:


\n

W=U​Σ​V⊤,σ1​(W)≥⋯≥σd​(W)≥0.W=U\Sigma V^{\top},\qquad igma_{1}(W)\geq\cdots\geq igma_{d}(W)\geq 0.


\nThe rule orders singular values decreasingly, chooses an orthonormal basis inside each singular subspace by a fixed deterministic convention, and fixes column signs by a fixed deterministic sign convention. All physical transport matrices, row groups, active columns, pairwise triples, and ICM structures below are defined relative to this chosen SVD gauge.

\n
\nIf a singular value has multiplicity greater than one, the individual singular vectors inside the corresponding eigenspace are not intrinsic. The intrinsic object is the singular subspace. The deterministic convention above makes the finite matrices reproducible, while the stability theorems require additional active-column, pairwise-margin, and perturbation inequalities precisely to ensure that the extracted incidence structure is stable for the chosen realization. The main statements below are therefore gauge-relative finite-dimensional certificates for this fixed, reproducible SVD gauge unless a separate singular-subspace gap assumption is imposed. A gauge-invariant formulation can instead be written in terms of orthogonal projectors PU=Uℐ​Uℐ⊤P_{U}=U_{\mathcal{I}}U_{\mathcal{I}}^{\top} and PV=Vℐ​Vℐ⊤P_{V}=V_{\mathcal{I}}V_{\mathcal{I}}^{\top} for singular-value clusters, with projector perturbations controlled by standard subspace perturbation estimates. We keep the gauge-fixed version because the measured physical matrices in Section 10 are computed from a deterministic SVD convention, but all stability conclusions should be interpreted relative to that convention.


\n

heading: Remark 4.2 (Vector-level versus projector-level stability).
text:
\n
\nThe gauge-fixed vector-level transports are most stable when the singular directions used individually are separated. heading: 4.2 Mode-profile grouping and active-support extraction
text:
\n
\nThe physical alignment structure makes the row and support choices explicit. It consists of row groups and active supports that can be extracted from static SVD data or proposed by a deterministic numerical routine. Definition 4.6 gives one sufficient, margin-stable row-assignment rule. When cosine or spectral clustering is used in the figures, the clustering step is treated as a fixed, predeclared proposal of the partition; the formal certificate is computed after that partition is fixed and the relevant margins are measured. No theorem below treats an arbitrary post-hoc clustering as intrinsically stable unless the corresponding row-profile or clustering eigengap margins are supplied.

\n

heading: Theorem 5.10 (Static channel incidence structure from physical alignment).
text:
\n
\nLet M^\widehat{M} carry a physical alignment structure with fixed row groups and active column sets.
Assume that all nondegenerate signal pairs satisfy the one-third threshold and that ‖Mnoise‖F≤εnoise\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}\|_{F}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}.
Then the margin-verified interface has the following static channel incidence structure:

\n(T1) 
\n
\nthe signal part decomposes into exclusive core blocks and controlled shared-support blocks;

\n(T2) 
\n
\ncoherent cross-talk between any pair is bounded by its exclusive margin;

\n(T3) 
\n
\nunstructured interaction outside core and shared support has Frobenius energy at most εnoise\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}};

\n(T4) 
\n
\nthe total energy splits according to (56).


\nMoreover, with the row groups and active column sets held fixed, if perturbations obey (51) for every pair and the noise perturbation has Frobenius norm at most ηF\eta_{F}, then the same fixed-support incidence certificate remains valid with noise bound εnoise+ηF\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}+\eta_{F}. If the active column sets are re-extracted after perturbation, the additional active-column gap condition of Theorem 7.3(C1) is also required.


\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nWe prove the four stated incidence-structure conclusions and then the perturbative assertion.

\n(T1) 
\n
\nExclusive core blocks and shared-support blocks.
The row partition and active-column sets are part of the physical alignment structure in Definition 4.17. For every signal pair i<ji<j, Definition 4.19 decomposes the pairwise columns into exclusive pieces 𝒞i∖𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{i} etminus\mathcal{C}_{j} and 𝒞j∖𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{j} etminus\mathcal{C}_{i} and a shared piece 𝒞i∩𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}. The corresponding submatrices are precisely Corei∖j\mathrm{Core}_{i etminus j}, Corej∖i\mathrm{Core}_{j etminus i}, and Overlapi∩j\mathrm{Overlap}_{i\cap j}. Globally, Definition 5.3 collects the columns active for exactly one signal group into McoreM_{\mathrm{core}} and the columns shared by at least two signal groups into MoverlapM_{\mathrm{overlap}}. Hence the signal part is a union of exclusive core blocks and controlled shared-support blocks.

\n(T2) 
\n
\nCoherent cross-talk is bounded by exclusive margins.
By hypothesis, every nondegenerate signal pair satisfies the one-third threshold. For such a pair,


\n

‖Overlapi∩j‖2=oi,j<13​mi,j.\|\mathrm{Overlap}_{i\cap j}\|_{2}=o_{i,j}<\frac{1}{3}m_{i,j}.


\nLemma 5.1 shows this is equivalent to the gap condition


\n

oi,j<12​Δσ​(i,j).o_{i,j}<\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{ igma}(i,j).


\nThus the coherent operator-norm cross-talk carried by the shared support of the pair is strictly smaller than both the one-third exclusive margin and one-half of the induced gap. Degenerate pairs have zero exclusive margin by definition and lie outside the pairwise stability condition.

\n(T3) 
\n
\nUnstructured interaction is bounded.
Definition 5.3 defines


\n

Mnoise=M^−Mcore−Moverlap.M_{\mathrm{noise}}=\widehat{M}-M_{\mathrm{core}}-M_{\mathrm{overlap}}.


\nThe theorem assumes ‖Mnoise‖F≤εnoise\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}\|_{F}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}. Therefore every coordinate not assigned to exclusive core or structured shared support has total Frobenius energy at most εnoise2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{2} and Frobenius norm at most εnoise\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}.

\n(T4) 
\n
\nEnergy splitting.
Proposition 5.7 states that the three coordinate masks defining McoreM_{\mathrm{core}}, MoverlapM_{\mathrm{overlap}}, and MnoiseM_{\mathrm{noise}} are disjoint. Therefore the three matrices are orthogonal for the Frobenius inner product. Applying the Pythagorean identity in the Frobenius Hilbert space gives


\n

‖M^‖F2=‖Mcore‖F2+‖Moverlap‖F2+‖Mnoise‖F2,\|\widehat{M}\|_{F}^{2}=\|M_{\mathrm{core}}\|_{F}^{2}+\|M_{\mathrm{overlap}}\|_{F}^{2}+\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}\|_{F}^{2},


\nwhich is (56).


\nFor the perturbation statement, the coordinate masks are interpreted as fixed. Assume each pairwise perturbation obeys (51). Theorem 5.2 then implies that every perturbed nondegenerate pair still satisfies the one-third threshold on those fixed blocks, so the fixed pairwise support relations and the controlled-overlap inequalities remain valid. If the active sets are re-selected from the perturbed matrix, one must additionally impose the active-column gap condition from Theorem 7.3(C1). If the perturbation of the noise component has Frobenius norm at most ηF\eta_{F}, then


\n

‖Mnoise′‖F≤‖Mnoise‖F+‖Mnoise′−Mnoise‖F≤εnoise+ηF.\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}^{\,\prime}\|_{F}\leq\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}\|_{F}+\|M_{\mathrm{noise}}^{\,\prime}-M_{\mathrm{noise}}\|_{F}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}+\eta_{F}.


\nThus the same incidence structure persists with the stated enlarged noise bound.
∎

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nWe prove the three claims by reducing each view to one of the stability theorems already established.

\n(V1) 
\n
\nSame-grid views.
Fix q∈𝒬sameq\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{same}}. The hypotheses give


\n

M^(q)=M^(0)+E(q),‖E(q)‖F≤ηq,\widehat{M}^{(q)}=\widehat{M}^{(0)}+E^{(q)},\qquad\|E^{(q)}\|_{F}\leq\eta_{q},


\nand assume exactly the active-column and pairwise-margin conditions (93)–(94). Theorem 7.12 therefore applies with reference index q0=0q_{0}=0. It yields equality of active column sets, equality of the pairwise support graph, equality of the core/overlap/noise coordinate masks, and preservation of the one-third coherent-overlap threshold for every nondegenerate pair. Since qq was arbitrary, the conclusion holds for all same-grid views.

\n(V2) 
\n
\nCompatible coarsened views.
Let q′∈𝒬coarseq^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{coarse}} be obtained from some q∈𝒬sameq\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{same}} by a compatible coarsening. By Definition 6.21, each coarse block is a disjoint union of fine blocks. Proposition 6.22(K2) states that if the coarse bad-block set is the image of the fine bad-block set under the coarsening maps, then the unnormalized bad energy of the coarsened view is no larger than the unnormalized bad energy of the fine view. Applying that result to the bad-block family ℬbad(q)\mathcal{B}^{(q)}_{\mathrm{bad}} gives the asserted bound on the coarsened unnormalized bad energy. The corresponding unweighted row-normalized heatmap sum need not be monotone under coarsening unless additional row-energy balance assumptions are imposed; this is why the statement uses the Frobenius-energy version.

\n(V3) 
\n
\nFinite-family aggregation.
By (V1), all same-grid views determine one common finest-grid support graph, active-set family, pairwise one-third margin family, and core/overlap/noise mask family. By (V2), every compatible coarsened view is obtained from this finest-grid structure by deterministic aggregation and cannot increase the measured bad mass on the induced bad blocks. Thus the entire finite family of views represents the same margin-stable static GSA structure together with its compatible coarse images. The stable mathematical content is exactly the data invariant under these operations: the support graph, the core/overlap/noise decomposition, the pairwise coherent-overlap margins, and the block-energy structure.


\n∎

heading: Proposition 7.17 (Finite measurement family under the geometric hypotheses).
text:
\n
\nAssume a chain satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 2.11, the rank-window separation hypotheses of Corollary 2.26, and the dynamic-to-static hypotheses of Theorem 7.2. Assume further that the physical matrices in the measurement family satisfy the active-column and pairwise-margin separation hypotheses of Theorem 7.12, and that the scale-free/energy-weighted paired views satisfy the positive diagonal conditioning hypothesis of Proposition 6.18. Then the following finite-dimensional predictions hold.

\n(P1) 
\n
\nSpectral-coordinate shortness.
The sequence 𝔄spec=(α^k)\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{spec}}=(\hat{\alpha}_{k}) has total variation bounded by the local interface budget, with the constants of Theorem 2.11 and the robust correction of Theorem 2.13 when the power-law fit is approximate.

\n(P3)

\n(P5)

For the depth-indexed family 𝔄depth\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{depth}}, the static GSA structural system persists across all depths satisfying the perturbation, active-gap, and pairwise-gap bounds of Theorem 7.12. Compatible coarse visualizations inherit the same structure through Proposition 6.22.

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nEach component of the measurement family is a finite collection of deterministic quantities computed from static layer matrices. We prove the five claims one by one.

\n(P1) 
\n
\nSpectral-coordinate shortness.
The component 𝔄spec\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{spec}} is the fitted coordinate sequence (α^k)(\hat{\alpha}_{k}). Theorem 2.13 gives local and total-variation bounds in terms of the interface budgets log⁡λk\log\lambda_{k} and chart errors. \n(P2)

\nStable rank windows.
The component 𝔄rank\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{rank}} consists of energy-rank windows. \n(P3) 
\n
\nBlock-sparse static channel incidence structure.
The component 𝔄phys\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{phys}} contains permuted physical alignment matrices and their block-energy matrices. By the assumed active-column and pairwise-margin separations, Theorem 7.12 gives equality of active sets, pairwise support graphs, and core/overlap/noise masks across the physical views. \nunder the row-energy hypotheses in that theorem. Thus small plotted bad mass provides a numerical upper bound on the measured off-structure Frobenius energy.

\n(P4)

\nScale-free/energy-weighted consistency.
If a paired scale-free and energy-weighted view has the form B=Dr​A​DcB=D_{r}AD_{c} in the displayed coordinates, Proposition 6.18 bounds every block energy by the factor


\n

Θ=(a+​b+a−​b−)2,\Theta=\left(\frac{a_{+}b_{+}}{a_{-}b_{-}}\right)^{2},

For output-realized physical-row panels, the singular-value weighting generally acts through LR=Uk+1(R)​Σk+1(R)​(Uk+1(R))⊤L_{R}=U_{k+1}^{(R)}\Sigma_{k+1}^{(R)}(U_{k+1}^{(R)})^{\top} rather than through a diagonal row scaling; in that case Proposition 6.20 gives the replacement bound with an explicit row-leakage and bad-column multiplicity term. The depth-indexed component 𝔄depth\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{depth}} is a finite family of physical matrices over layer index. For views displayed at compatible coarse resolutions, Proposition 6.22 proves that the coarse block-energy structure is the row-energy weighted aggregation of the fine one and that bad mass does not increase under compatible coarsening. \n

heading: 9 Low-disruption fine-tuning paths in GSA coordinates
text:
\n
\nThe preceding sections extract static channel structure from a trained model. We now record two finite-dimensional consequences for local adaptation. The goal is not to model a particular optimizer. Instead, we identify the scale and singular-frame directions that have small displacement in the static GSA coordinates. This gives a precise version of two matrix-level low-disruption conditions: uniform spectral scaling and coherent singular-vector rotation. These coordinates can be used to analyze a given adapter, LoRA, or other local update after it has been measured, but the statements below do not prove that any particular fine-tuning method automatically preserves GSA structure.

heading: Remark 9.5 (Deep-learning interpretation).
text:
\n
\nProposition 9.2 identifies uniform layerwise scaling as the zero-disruption scale direction. Proposition 9.4 identifies the corresponding directional condition: if a fine-tuned layer remains close to the base layer in Frobenius norm, and if its common frame rotation does not mix widely separated singular directions, then the output and input singular-vector rotations must be close to one another. In channel terms, low-disruption adaptation preserves the layer’s input-output frame up to a coherent rotation and avoids arbitrary re-wiring of the dominant singular directions.

heading: 10 Empirical measurements of the finite-dimensional predictions
text:
\n
\nThe experiments are organized by the finite-dimensional variables appearing in the theorems. The spectral measurements track the fitted Cartan coordinate. The physical-alignment measurements build the transport matrices and their block-energy summaries. The effective-rank measurements compare whether the same block structure persists under different spectral truncation windows. This organization separates three levels of empirical measurements: spectral evolution, channel organization, and stability of the observed organization under changes of the retained rank window.

heading: Operator and protocol reporting.
text:
\n
\nA reproducible certificate report must state the extraction protocol ℰ\mathcal{E} of Definition 8.3. In particular, it must identify the measured operator for each architecture: for transformers, which attention or MLP matrices are used, or whether a composed interface block is measured; for convolutional networks, how convolution kernels are flattened and whether normalization layers are folded into the matrix; and for diffusion or vision backbones, which linearized block is treated as WkW_{k}. The report must also state whether the displayed columns are source singular modes or physical input channels, following Table 3.

heading: Null and randomization baselines.
text:
\n
\nBecause permutations and clustering can create visually organized displays, the same extraction pipeline should also be run on null controls before making an empirical membership claim. Recommended controls include random Gaussian matrices with matched dimensions, matrices with the same singular values but random singular vectors, trained weights with randomly permuted channels, untrained initialization, random orthogonal rotations of singular frames, and the same clustering pipeline applied to null data. A Physical GSA certificate should report whether the measured margins distinguish the trained interface from these controls.

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nWe prove the four assertions.

\n
\nFor (V1), Theorem 2.13 states that the total variation of the Cartan coordinate is bounded by the measured local transport budgets and chart errors. The quantity D^spec\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{spec}} is exactly the left-hand side of that total-variation estimate with the fitted coordinates replacing the theoretical coordinates. Thus, once the fit errors are included in the chart-error term, it is the empirical instance of the theorem’s spectral residual.

\n
\nFor (V2), Definition 8.6 defines the physical GSA residual as the sum of the spectral total variation, the Frobenius norms of the noise components, and the positive parts of the one-third-threshold violations over nondegenerate pairs. The quantities D^noise\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{noise}} and D^pair\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{pair}} are precisely the second and third terms of that definition computed from the measured physical structures.

\n
\nFor (V3), Proposition 8.7 gives an upper bound for the sum of the three residuals in Definition 8.6. Substituting the measured budgets, chart errors, noise norms, and pairwise margins into that proposition yields the asserted finite-dimensional margin test. The conclusion is conditional on the same hypotheses as the proposition: the rank windows, physical structures, nondegenerate-pair convention, and overlap margin assumptions must be evaluated on the same objects that produced the figures.

\n
\nFor (V4), Theorem 7.3 proves that active-column sets, pairwise incidence structure, and the derived core/overlap/noise and SRS/Hub incidence structures are unchanged under perturbations whose size is below the specified active-column and pairwise margin thresholds. The active-column inequality in the statement is exactly the stability condition used to preserve selected support sets. When the one-third threshold is not measured directly but inferred from a block-energy heatmap, Proposition 6.8 converts the numerical screen ei​Ei​j+ej​Ej​i<mi,j2/9e_{i}E_{ij}+e_{j}E_{ji}<m_{i,j}^{2}/9 into 3​‖Overlapi∩j‖2<mi,j3\|\mathrm{Overlap}_{i\cap j}\|_{2}<m_{i,j}. Therefore, if these inequalities hold for the measured perturbation sizes ηk\eta_{k}, the extracted SRS/Hub/core-overlap-noise anatomy is stable under the corresponding truncation and full-transport error, and the full SC/SA/ST ICM labels are stable once the additional row/profile margins are verified.
∎

heading: 11 Conclusion
text:
\n
\nThis article develops the angular and static-channel component of GSA. The spectral results imported from the companion article identify a stable dominant energy window. Inside that window, angular transport matrices and their physical realizations produce finite static objects: the Physical Alignment Matrix, block-energy matrices, pairwise relational triples, the core/overlap/noise decomposition, and ICM/SRS/Hub variables. The deterministic theorems specify when these objects are stable under truncation error, diagonal reweighting, full-transport perturbations, and pairwise overlap perturbations. The same coordinates yield low-disruption fine-tuning consequences: small scale-ratio cost forces uniform layerwise scaling, while small SVD-frame displacement and low common-frame cost force coherent left/right singular-vector rotations.

\n
\nThe alignment experiments are placed next to the corresponding finite quantities. They measure whether trained models display the predicted block-dominant physical transport and whether the same structure persists across effective-rank windows, cluster choices, and layer sweeps. The visual matrices give measurements consistent with the qualitative structural pattern; the finite-dimensional margin checking is obtained by reporting and checking the associated numerical margins. Together with the spectral article, this gives a two-part GSA certificate theory: the spectral article controls the location and motion of the dominant spectral window, and this article gives finite-dimensional margin conditions under which the channel-incidence structure transported inside that window is stable and represents a controlled approximation to the full interface transport.
